title: Here’s How to Overcome Student Speaking Anxiety
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart tells the story of Kym, a ninth grader convinced she could not speak in class, to lay out a seven-step approach to student public-speaking anxiety. The sequence starts with warm-calling in week one (written answer, peer share, then random call), supported by research on cold-calling and by the need to normalize participation early. It continues with deliberate connection to anxious students, a first pop-up debate after about three weeks with advance coaching for the nervous ones, specific praise after success, and a show-of-hands poll revealing that most students feel nervous. His argument is that teachers owe anxious students systematic instruction and expectation in speaking, just as a swim instructor owes students water safety, and that Kym's thanks years later came from being expected to speak, not from heroics. Stuart also admits he shares Kym's introversion.
points: Warm-calling, with a short written answer and a peer share before the teacher calls on someone at random, gets every student speaking in week one without cold shock.
Participation norms have to be set early, because a classroom culture that is established around silence is hard to change later.
Anxious students need targeted connection and advance coaching, such as being told success is simply reading their warm-up writing aloud.
A visual poll showing most students feel nervous breaks the illusion that anxiety is unique to the individual.
Stuart's claim is that the teacher's care is shown through structured conditions that teach and expect speaking, not through exemption.
quotes: But students’ minds needn’t be stone cold on a question before you call on them. Rather, I find it’s best to have students first answer a question (briefly) in writing, and then to have them share the gist of what they’ve written with a peer, and then to work through your roster calling them at random.

Normalize participation early and often. As Martha Sevetson Rush writes in Beat Boredom: Engaging Tuned-Out Teenagers, “Once a classroom culture is established, it is difficult to change, so lecturing for six weeks and then suddenly calling on students to discuss will result in an uncomfortable silence” (73).

Once a student indicates to me that they are anxious about speaking publicly (as Kym did via email, or this past year as Chris did when he refused to speak during a Week 1 warm-call), I take extra pains to connect with them via moments of genuine connection. My goal is to make them feel valued, known, and respected.
Where possible, I speak to their anxiety around public speaking during these moments, and about how this is actually normal. I sometimes share how this was my own struggle in school, too.
I’m explicit before the debate starts: this will happen! And all you need to do in this situation is read from the writing you did at the start of class.
This is a weird thing about anxiety — it convinces us that we’re the only ones experiencing it! But actually, it is normal to feel some trepidation about speaking in front of one’s peers.
